stemMd:
Regional librarian: Across the region, the branch libraries that extended their opening hours into the evening lent 12 percent more items in the following year than they had in the year before. Extending opening hours into the evening therefore causes a library's lending to rise.

Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the librarian's argument?

options.label: A
options.textMd: In the prior year, lending had been flat both at the branches that later extended their hours and at comparable branches that never did.

options.label: B
options.textMd: The 12 percent figure was measured, for each branch, over the twelve months immediately following the date its evening hours began.

options.label: C
options.textMd: The branches that extended their evening hours held larger and more recently updated collections, on average, than the branches that did not.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Most items borrowed during the new evening hours were borrowed by regular patrons who had previously done their borrowing during the day.

options.label: E
options.textMd: The branches that extended their evening hours also enlarged their acquisitions budgets and bought many new titles in the same year.

explanationMd:
A causal conclusion drawn from a before-and-after comparison is exposed on two flanks. The rise might reflect a trend already under way (the branches were growing anyway), and the branches that chose to extend might have been different from the rest in ways that explain the rise (selection). A strengthener is any fact that closes one of those flanks.

The choice about lending having been flat in the prior year at both the extending and the non-extending branches closes both at once. "Flat ... at the branches that later extended their hours" kills the pre-existing-trend story: these branches were not already climbing. "And at comparable branches that never did" supplies a control group: comparable libraries that made no change saw no rise, so whatever produced the 12 percent was not something happening to libraries generally that year. That is as close to a controlled comparison as an observational claim of this kind can get, and it is what makes that choice decisively the best answer.

Check your work by asking, for each choice, which way the argument moves once the fact is added.

- The choice about enlarged acquisitions budgets and many new titles introduces a rival cause operating at exactly the same time — the argument gets *weaker*.
- The choice about most evening borrowers being regular patrons who had previously borrowed by day suggests borrowing was merely rescheduled from daytime to evening, which is consistent with total lending not being driven up by the change at all — weaker again.
- The choice about the twelve-month measurement window is a definition of the measurement window. It tells you what was counted, not why it rose.
- The choice about larger and more recently updated collections at the extending branches says those branches differed systematically from the others, which is the selection problem itself, not a cure for it.

The habit worth keeping: on a strengthen question for a causal claim, look first for a choice that rules out an alternative explanation or supplies a comparison group, and be suspicious of any choice that adds a second thing that changed at the same time.

distractorRationale.e: A larger acquisitions budget and a wave of new titles are a rival explanation for the rise in lending, operating in the same branches in the same year. Adding them makes the causal conclusion harder to sustain, not easier. It is tempting because it names a plausible driver of library use, but a strengthener must remove competitors rather than introduce one.
distractorRationale.d: If the evening borrowers are mostly regular patrons who used to borrow in the daytime, the evening figures may represent lending moved rather than lending created, which puts pressure on the claim that the extension raised total lending. This is a weakener dressed in the vocabulary of the new evening hours.
distractorRationale.b: This merely specifies the measurement window and adds no evidence about causation. Every explanation of the rise, including a pre-existing trend or a region-wide surge, is equally compatible with the figure being measured over the twelve months after each branch's evening hours began. A fact that no rival hypothesis would contest cannot discriminate between hypotheses.
distractorRationale.c: This states that the two groups of branches differed before the change, which is the selection problem the argument most needs to escape. Larger and fresher collections are an obvious alternative source of higher lending, so the choice supplies a confound rather than eliminating one.

accessibilityText: A short causal argument. Branch libraries that extended opening hours into the evening lent 12 percent more items in the following year than in the year before, and the librarian concludes that extending evening hours causes lending to rise. The question asks which statement, if true, most strengthens the argument. Five answer choices, labelled A through E. No notation, tables or figures appear.

provenance.notes: Original stimulus and choices. Strengthen item on a before-and-after causal claim; the key supplies both a flat pre-trend and an untreated comparison group, while two distractors are weakeners and two are inert. Not derived from any published LSAT item.

review.author: lsat-wave3-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The argument is a before-after comparison; showing lending was flat in the prior year at the extending branches (and at comparable non-extending ones) rules out a pre-existing upward trend as the source of the 12 percent rise. Measuring the window from the date evening hours began only marginally aligns timing; larger collections and enlarged acquisitions budgets offer alternative causes (weaken); regulars merely shifting their borrowing to the evening undercuts the causal claim. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-cue-batch1-run1) reached the same answer: The argument is a before/after comparison; showing that lending had been flat beforehand at the extending branches (and at comparable non-extending branches) rules out a pre-existing upward trend as the explanation for the 12 percent rise. Larger collections and enlarged acquisitions budgets are confounds (weaken); regulars merely shifting borrowing time suggests displacement rather than new lending; aligning the measurement window to the start date only tidies timing and does not address alternative causes.]
